section_summary: This section concerns Japan’s economic stabilization, trade, unemployment, and the gradual transfer of economic administration from the Occupation to Japanese authorities. It includes policy papers, correspondence about the Dodge program, and Tokyo reports on trade agreements, shipping, securities exchanges, and Occupation controls. Several documents are duplicate record copies; the final memorandum continues beyond page 576.

subfiles.title: Unidentified concluding page on stabilization funding
subfiles.about: Possible funds for unemployment measures after reparations removals cease.
subfiles.summary: The concluding page identifies unused reparations funds as a possible source for unemployment measures.

subfiles.title: Public Relations Aspects of the Economic Stabilization Program in Japan
subfiles.about: How education and economic incentives might build support for Japan’s stabilization program.
subfiles.summary: The paper argues that misunderstanding and hardship threaten support for stabilization and the prestige of the Occupation. It proposes public education about recovery and U.S. aid, alongside cotton goods, tax relief, flexible wages, and unemployment measures. Possible funding includes reduced Occupation costs, counterpart funds, and unused reparations appropriations.

subfiles.title: Request to acknowledge Admiral Toyoda’s letter
subfiles.about: Preparation of an acknowledgment for Grew’s forwarded correspondence.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth requests a draft acknowledgment of Toyoda’s letter and enclosure.

subfiles.title: Grew’s letter forwarding Toyoda’s correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwarding Toyoda’s letter and private opinion for discreet handling.
subfiles.summary: Grew forwards Toyoda’s materials and asks that his situation be handled discreetly.

subfiles.title: Resume of Private Opinion
subfiles.about: Measures Toyoda considers necessary alongside the Dodge budget.
subfiles.summary: Toyoda urges action on communism, labor, unemployment, food, shipping, reparations, and industrial advice. He warns that a financial program alone could fail and strengthen communism.

subfiles.title: Toyoda to Grew
subfiles.about: Toyoda’s concerns about Japan’s economy, politics, and relationship with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Toyoda describes his purge and his fears about communist gains and declining Japanese confidence. He calls for a broadly empowered American economic adviser and closer U.S.–Japanese relations.

subfiles.title: Butterworth to Grew
subfiles.about: Acknowledging Grew’s letter and promising source protection.
subfiles.summary: Butterworth thanks Grew and promises to protect Toyoda’s identity in any use of the material.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about a Dodge Mission report
subfiles.about: Whether the Dodge Mission would publish its recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Littlejohn asks whether and when a Dodge Mission report will be available.

subfiles.title: Reply on Dodge Mission publications
subfiles.about: Explaining that no comprehensive Dodge Mission report is planned.
subfiles.summary: McDiarmid says the mission issued press releases but plans no comprehensive published report.

subfiles.title: Partly illegible incoming economic airgram
subfiles.about: A multi-page economic report whose substantive text is largely unreadable.
subfiles.summary: The surviving OCR permits only fragmentary identification of economic and trade matters.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-163
subfiles.about: Updates on foreign creditors, trade, transport, and export rules.
subfiles.summary: The airgram discusses accounts for foreign creditors, Sterling Area trade, Soviet coal negotiations, a proposed Naha airline stop, country-of-origin marking, and technical information requests. Portions are difficult to read.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on discussion of Japan with Ambassador Franks
subfiles.about: Transmitting proposed memoranda on reparations, gold, and trade.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum forwards draft material responding to issues raised by Bevin.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Bevin
subfiles.about: A discussion of Japanese economic questions.
subfiles.summary: The heavily damaged OCR indicates discussion of Japanese trade and related economic policy.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-173
subfiles.about: Recent trade arrangements and other economic developments.
subfiles.summary: The partly illegible report addresses Sterling Area trade, proposed arrangements, and related commercial concerns.

subfiles.title: Nanking telegram on Japanese economic policy
subfiles.about: A reported plan concerning Japanese economic revival.
subfiles.summary: The damaged telegram refers to U.S. funds, raw materials, productivity, and Japanese recovery.

subfiles.title: Instruction to repeat Nanking telegram
subfiles.to: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Repeating Nanking’s July 7 telegram for information.
subfiles.summary: The Department instructs that Nanking’s telegram be repeated to SCAP and its information section.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-176
subfiles.about: Trade, securities exchanges, air routes, shipping, pearls, and private imports.
subfiles.summary: The report covers Swiss trade, the opening of regional securities exchanges, a proposed British air route, a shipping conference dispute, pearl sales, overseas trade offices, private importing, and renewal of the Sterling Area arrangement.

subfiles.title: DuBois memorandum forwarding stabilization paper
subfiles.about: Sending copies of a paper and draft covering memorandum.
subfiles.summary: DuBois sends six copies of the requested paper and a draft memorandum.

subfiles.title: Duplicate DuBois forwarding memorandum
subfiles.about: A second copy of the paper’s forwarding memorandum.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats DuBois’s transmittal of six copies and a draft memorandum.

subfiles.title: Draft transmittal of stabilization paper
subfiles.about: Forwarding an informal paper for possible Army and SCAP interest.
subfiles.summary: The draft describes the attached paper as informal and potentially useful to Army or SCAP officers.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of stabilization paper
subfiles.about: Sending the informal stabilization paper.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the transmittal’s description of the paper as informal.

subfiles.title: Partly illegible filed document
subfiles.about: A filed document with largely unreadable text.
subfiles.summary: The OCR is insufficient to identify its argument or correspondents reliably.

subfiles.title: Replacement record-copy slip
subfiles.about: Designating a replacement record copy of a Tokyo despatch.
subfiles.summary: The slip marks a copy as the record copy because the original action copy was not returned.

subfiles.title: Despatch 457 forwarding conversation on current economic problems
subfiles.about: Forwarding Maynard’s July 8 conversation with Freile.
subfiles.summary: Maynard and Freile discuss Japan’s living standards, sales, and reorganization of SCAP economic work. They also consider trade arrangements, export floor prices, private imports, foreign exchange incentives, shipping, trade offices, currencies, and pearls. Both favor reducing direct Occupation management.

subfiles.title: Boehringer letter about despatch 457
subfiles.about: Requesting restricted handling of despatch 457.
subfiles.summary: Boehringer asks that the despatch be marked for Department use only.

subfiles.title: Action copy of despatch 457 and enclosure
subfiles.about: A duplicate action copy of the Freile–Maynard economic discussion.
subfiles.summary: The duplicate records their views on SCAP staffing, trade agreements, export prices, imports, shipping, currencies, and pearls. They recommend greater Japanese responsibility and a smaller advisory role for Occupation economic staff.

subfiles.title: Reedy summary of Tokyo despatch 457
subfiles.about: Summarizing the Freile–Maynard discussion.
subfiles.summary: Reedy summarizes proposals for reduced SCAP staffing, stronger sales, trade promotion, and fewer controls.

subfiles.title: Request to restrict despatch 457
subfiles.about: Adding a Department-use-only designation to despatch 457.
subfiles.summary: The mission urgently asks for restricted distribution of the confidential despatch.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-185
subfiles.about: Hokkaido conditions and current trade and export questions.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Hokkaido’s relative prosperity, development pressures, and fishing concerns. It also covers Sterling Area negotiations, trade with Sweden and Pakistan, export contract rules, floor prices, and worries about reduced Occupation oversight of crop and tax collection.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-189
subfiles.about: Reduced directives and staffing, trade negotiations, imports, claims, and unemployment.
subfiles.summary: The airgram reports cancellation of SCAP directives, contraction of Eighth Army civil affairs work, and investigation of a claimed economic crisis. It surveys Soviet trade-office requests, Sterling Area and Latin American arrangements, delayed private imports, foreign property claims, and work relief.

subfiles.title: Tokyo economic airgram A-196
subfiles.about: Sterling Area procurement and related trade questions.
subfiles.summary: The damaged text refers to Japanese purchases of coal, sisal, jute, wool waste, and other Sterling Area goods.

subfiles.title: Despatch 544 transmitting Maynard’s decontrol memorandum
subfiles.about: Forwarding Maynard’s recommendations for progressive economic decontrol.
subfiles.summary: Sebald forwards Maynard’s personal assessment, emphasizing his experience with SCAP economic operations. The mission supports a coordinated reduction of Occupation personnel and an early return of economic administration to Japanese authorities, while retaining high-level policy oversight pending a peace settlement.

subfiles.title: Progressive Decontrol of the Economy of Japan
subfiles.about: An argument for rapid withdrawal of direct American economic controls.
subfiles.summary: Maynard argues that Japan’s industrial and financial capacity makes self-support possible if it faces the costs of its own economy. He urges that railways, shipping, coal, textiles, fishing, and food administration return to Japanese hands, with Occupation staff limited to inspection, advice, reporting, and essential financial controls. The memorandum continues after page 576.
